description: We are Alpha X, an independent team of five students participating in NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. Our team includes three BCA students, one BJMC student, and one B.Com student. We share interests in web development, digital media, business, and technology. Some members have practical experience, while others are enthusiastic beginners. We're creating a Space Mission Design Game to make space science fun and interactive. Our goal is to learn, collaborate, and innovate together. 🚀
summary:
Team Alpha X developed ORBICRAFT, a browser game that lets players design, launch, and operate fictional science missions around Earth, the Moon, and Mars. Players choose instruments, power systems, radios, orbits, and launch vehicles while balancing mass, budget, battery life, and data storage. During flight, they decide when to collect observations, conserve power, or transmit data. A mission report explains the results so players can revise their design and try again.

ORBICRAFT addresses the Space Mission Design Game challenge by connecting engineering choices to measurable outcomes. Its Earth mission, FIREWATCH-1, uses NASA’s four mission segments—launch, space, ground, and user—to show how wildfire observations travel from a spacecraft to researchers. The simulation uses illustrative values so players can focus on the trade-offs. By experimenting with different designs, students can see why collecting more data only helps when the spacecraft can also deliver it.
details:
Project Details

What we built
ORBICRAFT is an educational browser game by Team Alpha X. Players design, launch, and operate fictional science missions around Earth, the Moon, and Mars. Each destination presents a different engineering challenge.

How it works

  1. Design: Choose instruments, batteries, solar panels, a radio, an orbit, and a launch vehicle.
  2. Review: Check the spacecraft’s mass against the launcher’s capacity and make sure the design stays within budget.
  3. Operate: Decide when to collect observations, conserve battery power, or transmit data to the ground.
  4. Learn: Read the mission report, compare outcomes, and redesign the spacecraft for another attempt.

What makes it creative
The game lets players test how one engineering choice affects the entire mission. In two FIREWATCH-1 simulations, the same instrument collected 72 GB in each run. The high-capacity radio returned 58.32 useful GB, while the standard radio returned 17.50 useful GB. These illustrative results show why collecting observations is only part of the job. The spacecraft must have enough communication capacity to deliver them.

How we used NASA’s resource
NASA’s four mission segments guided the FIREWATCH-1 experience. The launch segment covers getting the spacecraft into orbit. The space segment covers collecting observations. The ground segment shows data received during contact windows. The user segment shows how much useful science reaches researchers. NASA’s Design and Develop Science Missions, slide 8

Intended impact
We designed ORBICRAFT to help students and beginners learn mission engineering by making decisions and seeing their consequences. Players consider mass, cost, battery reserves during eclipse, storage, communication windows, and mission duration. The Moon mission adds fuel and energy planning for arrival, and Mars adds delayed commands and onboard survival decisions. Mission Academy, the flight manual, and 2D viewing options help new players get started.

Tools we used
We built the game with React, TypeScript, and Vite, and used Three.js and React Three Fiber for the interactive spacecraft views and launch sequences. We used Git and GitHub for version control, Vercel for hosting, and Codex to assist with development and testing. Progress is saved in the browser.
